mk-wacc-apv-1.title: Valuation with leverage
mk-wacc-apv-1.merke: Samme form som prosjekteksemplet i forelesning 08 (WACC, deretter APV)
mk-wacc-apv-1.body:
Orvelle Appliances, a European kitchen-appliance maker, considers a countertop steam oven that it will sell for three years. Today is Year 0 and the project has the same risk as the firm. In market values Orvelle has equity of €540 million, debt of €385 million and excess cash of €25 million. It measures leverage with net debt (debt minus cash) and keeps its net debt-to-equity ratio constant, also with the project. Its cost of equity is 11%, its cost of debt 5% and the tax rate 25%.

€ millionYear 0Year 1Year 2Year 3
Sales609070
Cost of goods sold243628
Operating expenses121212
Launch costs8
Equipment purchase45

The launch costs are expensed in Year 0 and lower Orvelle's tax bill that year. The equipment is depreciated straight-line to zero over Years 1 to 3. There is no working capital. Use 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.body: Find the free cash flow of the project in each year.
parts.solution:
Use the formula-sheet definition FCF = EBIT(1 − τ) + Depreciation − CapEx − ΔNWC. The free cash flow is unlevered: no interest is subtracted, even though Orvelle has debt. The financing enters later, through the discount rate (WACC) or the tax shield (APV).

Step 1. Depreciation. 45/3 = 15 per year in Years 1 to 3.

Step 2. Year 0. The launch costs give EBIT = −8. Because Orvelle is profitable elsewhere, its tax bill falls by 0.25 × 8 = 2, so the after-tax cost is 8(1 − 0.25) = 6. With the equipment: FCF0 = −6 − 45 = −51.

Step 3. Years 1 to 3.

€ millionYear 0Year 1Year 2Year 3
Sales609070
− Cost of goods sold−24−36−28
− Operating expenses−12−12−12
− Launch costs−8
− Depreciation−15−15−15
EBIT−892715
− Tax (25%)2−2.25−6.75−3.75
EBIT(1 − τ)−66.7520.2511.25
+ Depreciation151515
− CapEx−45
FCF−5121.7535.2526.25

FCF0 = −51, FCF1 = 21.75, FCF2 = 35.25, FCF3 = 26.25 (€ million).
criteria: FCF is unlevered: no interest is subtracted. The lecturer warns against subtracting interest again and again (lectures 08 and 18).
Year 0: the launch costs lower the tax bill, so the after-tax cost is 8(1 − 0.25) = 6 and FCF_0 = −6 − 45 = −51. Writing −53 forgets the tax saving.
Depreciation of 15 per year is subtracted before tax and added back after tax. Forgetting to add it back gives 6.75, 20.25 and 11.25.
FCF = 21.75, 35.25 and 26.25 in Years 1 to 3. Show the calculation.

parts.label: b
parts.body: Find Orvelle's after-tax WACC.
criteria: Nets the excess cash against the debt (cash is negative debt): D = 385 − 25 = 360, V = 900, D/V = 0.4.
Using the gross debt of 385 gives D/V = 0.4162 and r_wacc = 7.98%, which loses a point.
Applies (1 − τ) to r_D only, never to r_E.

parts.label: c
parts.body: Find the NPV of the project using the WACC method. (If you could not solve (a), use FCF = −50, 24, 33 and 28. If you could not solve (b), use rwacc = 7.5%. Use them here and below.)
parts.solution:
Discount the free cash flows at rwacc. FCF0 is paid today and is not discounted. The tax shield is already in the discount rate, so nothing is added.

NPV = −51 + 21.75/1.081 + 35.25/1.0812 + 26.25/1.0813
= −51.0000 + 20.1203 + 30.1653 + 20.7803 = €20.0659 million

The present value of the future cash flows is 71.0659. The question asks for the NPV, so the investment of 51 must be subtracted.

With the fallbacks: 20.8657 (rwacc = 7.5%), 22.6072 (the fallback FCF) or 23.4205 (both).
criteria: Discounts at r_wacc = 8.10% with the right powers and does not discount FCF_0.
Gives the NPV, 20.0659, not the PV of the future cash flows (71.0659). Stopping at the PV loses a point.
Full marks with the fallbacks: 20.8657, 22.6072 or 23.4205.
Does not add a tax shield on top: the WACC already contains it.

parts.label: d
parts.body: Find the project's debt capacity (the extra net debt Orvelle must hold) at the end of Years 0, 1 and 2. Does Orvelle borrow or repay in Years 1 to 3?
parts.solution:
To keep its ratio constant Orvelle must hold debt equal to d = D/V = 0.4 of the project's value at every date: Dt = d × VLt. VLt is the value at date t of the cash flows that are still to come, so solve backwards at rwacc.

Step 1. Values.

VL3 = 0
VL2 = 26.25/1.081 = 24.2831
VL1 = (35.25 + 24.2831)/1.081 = 55.0722
VL0 = (21.75 + 55.0722)/1.081 = 71.0659

Step 2. Debt capacity.

€ millionYear 0Year 1Year 2Year 3
VLt71.065955.072224.28310.0000
Dt = 0.4 × VLt28.426422.02899.71320.0000
Change in debt−6.3975−12.3157−9.7132

Orvelle borrows €28.4264 million today because of the project. It then repays 6.3975 in Year 1, 12.3157 in Year 2 and the last 9.7132 in Year 3. The project's value falls as its cash flows are paid out, so the debt that keeps the ratio constant falls too.

Note that D0 is based on the value of the future cash flows (71.0659), not on the NPV or the investment (0.4 × 51 = 20.4): once the 51 has been spent, the future cash flows are what the project adds to the value of Orvelle's assets, as in the lecture example.

With the fallbacks: rwacc = 7.5%: 28.7463, 22.2023 and 9.7674; the fallback FCF: 29.0429, 21.7954 and 10.3608; both: 29.3682, 21.9708 and 10.4186.
criteria: Uses D_t = d × V^L_t with d = D/V = 0.4. Multiplying by D/E = 0.6667 is the classic slip.
V^L_t is the value of the cash flows still to come, found backwards at r_wacc: V^L_2 = 24.2831, V^L_1 = 55.0722, V^L_0 = 71.0659.
D_0 = 28.4264, D_1 = 22.0289, D_2 = 9.7132 (and D_3 = 0). Basing D_0 on the NPV (giving 8.0264), on the investment (0.4 × 51 = 20.4) or on V^U is wrong.
Says that Orvelle repays debt in every year from Year 1 to Year 3. Bonus, not required: why (the project winds down).

parts.label: e
parts.body: Find rU. Then, with the debt from (d), find the unlevered value of the project's future cash flows, the present value of the tax shields and the NPV using APV. Compare with (c).
parts.solution:
Step 1. rU. Under a constant ratio the pre-tax WACC is rU:

rU = (E/V)rE + (D/V)rD = 0.6000(0.1100) + 0.4000(0.0500) = 0.0660 + 0.0200 = 0.0860 (8.60%)

Step 2. Unlevered value. The same free cash flows, discounted at rU:

VU0 = 21.75/1.086 + 35.25/1.0862 + 26.25/1.0863 = 20.0276 + 29.8882 + 20.4946 = 70.4104

Step 3. Tax shields. TSt = τ × rD × Dt−1, with the debt from (d):

TS1 = 0.25 × 0.05 × 28.4264 = 0.3553
TS2 = 0.25 × 0.05 × 22.0289 = 0.2754
TS3 = 0.25 × 0.05 × 9.7132 = 0.1214

Orvelle keeps its ratio constant, so the debt moves with the project's value and the tax shields are as risky as the project. Discount them at rU, not at rD:

PV(TS) = 0.3553/1.086 + 0.2754/1.0862 + 0.1214/1.0863 = 0.3272 + 0.2335 + 0.0948 = 0.6555

Step 4. APV.

NPV = FCF0 + VU0 + PV(TS) = −51.0000 + 70.4104 + 0.6555 = €20.0659 million

Check. The WACC method in (c) gave 20.0659 and APV gives 20.0659. They match. This is a fixed point rather than two independent estimates, because the debt in APV came from the WACC values, but it catches the wrong rate on the tax shield and slips in the arithmetic.

With the fallbacks: rwacc = 7.5% gives PV(TS) = 0.6615 and NPV = 20.0719 (no longer equal to (c), because the fallback is not the true WACC). The fallback FCF gives VU = 71.9408, PV(TS) = 0.6664 and NPV = 22.6072. Both give PV(TS) = 0.6726 and NPV = 22.6134.
criteria: r_U = pre-tax WACC = 0.6(11%) + 0.4(5%) = 8.60%. Putting (1 − τ) here gives the WACC, not r_U.
V^U_0 = 70.4104: the same FCF discounted at r_U.
TS_t = τ × r_D × D_(t−1): 0.3553, 0.2754 and 0.1214. Using D_t instead of D_(t−1) is a slip.
Discounts the tax shields at r_U: PV(TS) = 0.6555; at r_D it would be 0.6931. Bonus, not required: saying why (under a constant ratio the debt moves with the project's value and the shield with it).
Full marks with the fallbacks: NPV = 20.0719 (7.5%), 22.6072 (fallback FCF, with V^U = 71.9408) or 22.6134 (both).

parts.label: f
parts.body: Compare rwacc from (b) with rU from (e). Where does the difference come from? What happens to it if Orvelle chooses a higher target leverage? Explain briefly.
parts.solution:
rwacc = 8.10% is lower than rU = 8.60%. The gap is (D/V)τrD = 0.4 × 0.25 × 0.05 = 0.0050, or half a percentage point.

The two formulas differ only by the factor (1 − τ) on the cost of debt. Interest is tax deductible, so debt is cheaper after tax than its 5%. The WACC method puts this tax saving into the discount rate. APV discounts at rU (business risk only) and adds the tax shields as a separate value. Both give the same NPV.

With a higher target leverage rU stays the same, because the business risk does not change, while D/V rises. The gap (D/V)τrD widens and rwacc falls: more of the financing earns the tax deduction. Without corporate taxes the two rates would be equal.

Also accepted: a WACC above rU would be an alarm bell for an error, as the lecturer pointed out in lecture 09.
criteria: States that r_wacc = 8.10% is below r_U = 8.60%, a gap of 0.5 percentage points.

Explains the gap by the tax deduction on interest: the only difference between the formulas is (1 − τ) on r_D, so the WACC holds the tax shield inside the rate while APV adds it separately. The formula (D/V)τr_D is not required.
Higher target leverage: r_U is unchanged (business risk), the gap widens and r_wacc falls. Saying r_U rises with leverage loses this point.
1 to 3 sentences per point are enough; no new calculation is needed.

mk-wacc-apv-2.title: Valuation
mk-wacc-apv-2.merke: Samme form som H2024 E5, med to sammenlignbare firmaer som i forelesning 09
mk-wacc-apv-2.body:
Corliss Markets, a US supermarket chain, plans a new division that will sell meal kits by subscription. The division's free cash flow is expected to be $26 million next year and to grow by 2.5% per year forever. The division will keep a constant debt-to-value ratio of 40% and its cost of debt is 6%. Meal kits carry very different risk from supermarkets, but two listed meal-kit companies have the same business risk as the division. Both keep their leverage ratios constant:

CratewellMealmont
LeverageD/E = 0.6D/V = 0.25
Debt beta00.36
Equity beta1.601.48

Use the average of the two unlevered betas. The tax rate is 21%, the risk-free rate is 4.5% and the expected return on the market portfolio is 10%. Use 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.body: Find the unlevered beta of each comparable.
parts.solution:
The comparables have different leverage, so their equity betas cannot be compared directly. Strip out the leverage with the formula-sheet weighting (without taxes): βU = (E/V)βE + (D/V)βD.

Cratewell. D/E = 0.6, so D/V = 0.6/1.6 = 0.3750 and E/V = 0.6250. Its debt beta is zero:
βU = 0.6250 × 1.60 + 0.3750 × 0 = 1.0000

Mealmont. D/V = 0.25 is already a weight:
βU = 0.75 × 1.48 + 0.25 × 0.36 = 1.1100 + 0.0900 = 1.2000
criteria: Converts Cratewell's D/E = 0.6 into D/V = 0.375 before weighting. Using 0.6 as the debt weight gives 0.64.
Mealmont: beta_U = 0.75 × 1.48 + 0.25 × 0.36 = 1.2000. Dropping the debt beta gives 1.1100 and understates the asset risk.
Weights without taxes, as on the formula sheet.

parts.label: b
parts.body: Find the unlevered cost of capital and the cost of equity of the division.
criteria: Averages the unlevered betas (1.1000), not the equity betas. Averaging the equity betas gives 1.5400 and mixes in the comparables' leverage.
r_U = 4.5% + 1.1 × 5.5% = 10.55%. Using the full market return of 10% as the premium is the trap.
Converts the division's D/V = 0.40 into D/E = 0.6667 before MM II. Plugging in 0.40 gives 12.37%.

parts.label: c
parts.body: Find the division's after-tax WACC. (If you could not solve (b), use rU = 10% here and below.)
criteria: Uses the division's own weights E/V = 0.6 and D/V = 0.4, with (1 − τ) on r_D only.
The shortcut r_U − (D/V)τr_D gives the same number and is a quick cross-check.
Full marks with the fallback r_U = 10%: r_wacc = 9.4960%.

parts.label: d
parts.body: What is the levered value of the division using the WACC method?
parts.solution:
The free cash flow is a growing perpetuity that starts next year:

VL = FCF1/(rwacc − g) = 26/(0.100460 − 0.0250) = 26/0.075460 = $344.5534 million

The tax shield is inside the WACC, so nothing is added.

With the fallback rU = 10%: VL = 26/(0.094960 − 0.025) = 371.6409.
criteria: Uses the growing-perpetuity formula with the after-tax WACC: 26/(0.10046 − 0.025).
V^L = 344.5534. Leaving out the growth gives 258.8095.
Does not add a tax shield on top of the WACC value.
Full marks with the fallback r_U = 10%: V^L = 371.6409.

parts.label: e
parts.body: How much debt will the division carry today and one year from now? Use this debt to find the present value of the interest tax shields and the levered value of the division with the APV method. Compare with (d).
parts.solution:
Step 1. Debt. Dt = 0.4 × VLt. One year from now the division is worth the perpetuity that then starts with FCF2 = 26 × 1.025. Its value has grown by 2.5% and the debt grows with it:

D0 = 0.4 × 344.5534 = $137.8214 million
VL1 = 26.65/0.075460 = 353.1672, so D1 = 0.4 × 353.1672 = $141.2669 million

A value-creating, growing division forces the firm to borrow more every year to keep the ratio constant.

Step 2. Tax shields. TS1 = τ × rD × D0 = 0.21 × 0.06 × 137.8214 = 1.7365. The shields grow at 2.5% with the debt (TS2 = 1.7800). Under a constant D/V the shields carry the division's business risk, so they are discounted at rU:

PV(TS) = TS1/(rU − g) = 0.21 × 0.06 × 137.8214/(0.1055 − 0.0250) = 21.5720

Step 3. APV.

VU = 26/(0.1055 − 0.0250) = 26/0.0805 = 322.9814
VL = VU + PV(TS) = 322.9814 + 21.5720 = $344.5534 million

Check. The WACC method in (d) gave 344.5534. The two methods agree. The debt came from the WACC value, so this is a fixed point, but it catches the wrong rate or the wrong growth on the tax shield.

With the fallback rU = 10%: D0 = 148.6564, D1 = 152.3728, PV(TS) = 24.9743 and VL = 371.6409.
criteria: D_0 = 0.4 × 344.5534 = 137.8214 and D_1 = 141.2669: the debt grows with the value at 2.5%. Keeping D_1 = D_0 breaks the constant ratio.

Discounts the shields at r_U and with growth: PV(TS) = 0.21 × 0.06 × 137.8214/(0.1055 − 0.025) = 21.5720. Without growth 16.4602, at r_D 49.6157. Bonus, not required: saying why (under a constant D/V the shield moves with the value).
Notes that APV equals the WACC value in (d).

parts.label: f
parts.body: Corliss's own after-tax WACC is 6.2%. The CFO suggests discounting the division's free cash flows at this rate instead. Would that overvalue or undervalue the division? Explain briefly why the comparables are used, without new calculations.
parts.solution:
It would overvalue the division. 6.2% is well below the division's own WACC of 10.0460%. A lower rate gives a higher value.

The discount rate must match the risk of the cash flows being valued, not the risk of the firm that owns them. Corliss's WACC reflects a supermarket chain, a stable business, while meal kits by subscription carry more systematic risk. Used for every project, the firm's own rate makes risky projects look better than they are, so Corliss could accept projects with a negative NPV at the correct rate.

The comparables are pure meal-kit companies, so their betas show the division's business risk. Their leverage differs from the division's, so they are unlevered first and the average βU is relevered at the division's own D/V of 40%.
criteria: Overvalue: 6.2% is below the division's r_wacc of 10.0460%. A lower rate gives a higher value.
Why: the rate must reflect the risk of the division's cash flows (meal kits), not of the firm that owns them (supermarkets).
Why comparables: pure plays in the same business show the business risk. They are unlevered because their leverage differs, then relevered at the division's D/V.
Bonus, not required: the consequence, that Corliss could take on negative-NPV projects.
No new calculation is needed. 1 to 2 sentences per point are enough.

mk-wacc-apv-3.title: Valuation with leverage
mk-wacc-apv-3.merke: Samme form som H2025 E4 og prosjekteksemplet i forelesning 08
mk-wacc-apv-3.body:
Brandholm Toys, a listed Danish toy maker, earns a free cash flow of DKK 230 million per year from its existing business. Its equity is worth DKK 1,680 million and its debt DKK 720 million. Brandholm keeps this debt-to-value ratio constant, also for new projects. Its equity beta is 1.30 and its cost of debt 5%. The risk-free rate is 2.5%, the expected market return 7.5% and the tax rate 22%.

Brandholm holds a two-year licence for toys based on an animated series, a project with the same risk as the existing business. Today is Year 0. In DKK million:

  • A design agency has already been paid 3 for the designs.
  • Moulds cost 60 today, are depreciated straight-line to zero over Years 1 and 2 and are worthless afterwards.
  • Sales are 140 in Year 1 and 160 in Year 2. Costs other than depreciation are 65% of sales.
  • Lost sales of Brandholm's own range cut the EBITDA of the existing business by 7 in each of Years 1 and 2.
  • The project's net working capital is 14 at the end of Year 0, 16 at the end of Year 1 and zero at the end of Year 2.

Use 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.body: Find Brandholm's cost of equity and its after-tax WACC.
criteria: r_E = 2.5% + 1.30 × 5% = 9.00%, with the market risk premium of 5%, not 7.5%.
Weights from market values: D/V = 720/2,400 = 0.3. Using D/E = 0.4286 as a weight is wrong.

parts.label: b
parts.body: Find the free cash flow of the project in Years 0, 1 and 2.
parts.solution:
Value the project, not the firm: only the incremental cash flows count. The DKK 230 million from the existing business is irrelevant. The DKK 3 million paid to the design agency is sunk: it is gone whether or not Brandholm makes the toys. The lost EBITDA on the existing range is an indirect effect of the project and is subtracted. No interest is subtracted.

FCF = EBIT(1 − τ) + Depreciation − CapEx − ΔNWC, with depreciation 60/2 = 30 per year and ΔNWC the change in working capital, not its level:

DKK millionYear 0Year 1Year 2
Sales140160
− Costs (65% of sales)−91−104
− Lost EBITDA, existing range−7−7
Incremental EBITDA4249
− Depreciation−30−30
EBIT1219
− Tax (22%)−2.64−4.18
EBIT(1 − τ)9.3614.82
+ Depreciation3030
− CapEx−60
NWC (level)14160
− ΔNWC−14−216
FCF−7437.3660.82

FCF0 = −74, FCF1 = 37.36, FCF2 = 60.82. In Year 2 the working capital of 16 is released, which is a cash inflow.
criteria: Leaves out the 230 of the existing business and the sunk 3 for the designs. Including the sunk cost gives FCF_0 = −77.
Subtracts the lost EBITDA of 7 per year before tax: incremental EBITDA = 42 and 49.
Depreciation of 30 per year is subtracted before tax and added back after tax.
Uses ΔNWC, not the level: −14 in Year 0, −2 in Year 1 and +16 in Year 2. Using the levels ('forgetting the delta') gives 23.36 and 44.82.
FCF = −74, 37.36 and 60.82. Show the calculation.

parts.label: c
parts.body: Find the NPV of the project using the WACC method. (If you could not solve (b), use FCF = −75, 36 and 62 here and below.)
parts.solution:
NPV = −74 + 37.36/1.0747 + 60.82/1.07472
= −74.0000 + 34.7632 + 52.6589 = DKK 13.4221 million

The present value of the future cash flows is 87.4221, but the question asks for the NPV, so the outlay of 74 today is included. The NPV is positive, so the project is worth doing.

With the fallback cash flows: NPV = −75 + 36/1.0747 + 62/1.07472 = 12.1783.
criteria: Discounts the project's FCF at r_wacc = 7.47% and includes FCF_0 undiscounted.
NPV = 13.4221. Stopping at the PV (87.4221) answers a different question and loses a point.
Values the project, not the firm: a firm value built on the 230 earns nothing here.
Full marks with the fallback cash flows: NPV = 12.1783.

parts.label: d
parts.body: Find the project's debt capacity today and the debt adjustment at the end of Year 1. Does Brandholm borrow or repay?
parts.solution:
To keep D/V = 0.3, the project must carry debt Dt = 0.3 × VLt, where VLt is the value of the cash flows still to come.

VL1 = 60.82/1.0747 = 56.5925, so D1 = 0.3 × 56.5925 = 16.9778
VL0 = (37.36 + 56.5925)/1.0747 = 87.4221, so D0 = 0.3 × 87.4221 = 26.2266

Brandholm raises DKK 26.2266 million of debt today: 0.3 of the value of the future cash flows, not 0.3 of the outlay (0.3 × 74 = 22.2). At the end of Year 1 the adjustment is D1 − D0 = 0.3 × (56.5925 − 87.4221) = 0.3 × (−30.8296) = −9.2489: Brandholm repays DKK 9.2489 million, because the value of what is left of the project falls once FCF1 has been paid out. The rest, 16.9778, is repaid at the end of Year 2.

With the fallback cash flows: D0 = 26.1535 and the adjustment is −8.8463.
criteria: D_t = 0.3 × V^L_t, with V^L_t the value of the cash flows still to come, discounted at r_wacc.
D_0 = 0.3 × 87.4221 = 26.2266. Basing it on the outlay (0.3 × 74 = 22.2), on the NPV or on V^U is wrong.
V^L_1 = 60.82/1.0747 = 56.5925, so D_1 = 16.9778 and the adjustment is −9.2489. Leaving FCF_1 inside V^L_1 is the classic mistake.
Says in words that Brandholm repays debt at the end of Year 1.
Full marks with the fallback cash flows: D_0 = 26.1535, adjustment −8.8463.

parts.label: e
parts.body: Find rU, the present value of the tax shields and the NPV using the APV method. Compare with (c).
parts.solution:
Step 1. rU. rU = (E/V)rE + (D/V)rD = 0.7000(0.0900) + 0.3000(0.0500) = 0.0630 + 0.0150 = 0.0780 (7.80%)

Step 2. Unlevered value. VU0 = 37.36/1.0780 + 60.82/1.07802 = 34.6568 + 52.3370 = 86.9938

Step 3. Tax shields on the debt from (d), paid on the debt at the start of each year:

TS1 = 0.22 × 0.05 × 26.2266 = 0.2885
TS2 = 0.22 × 0.05 × 16.9778 = 0.1868

The debt follows the project's value, so the shields carry the project's risk and are discounted at rU:

PV(TS) = 0.011 × 26.2266/1.0780 + 0.011 × 16.9778/1.07802 = 0.2676 + 0.1607 = 0.4283 (0.011 = 0.22 × 0.05)

Step 4. APV. NPV = FCF0 + VU0 + PV(TS) = −74.0000 + 86.9938 + 0.4283 = DKK 13.4221 million

Check. The WACC method in (c) gave 13.4221. The two NPVs agree, as they must when the debt follows Dt = d × VLt.

With the fallback cash flows: PV(TS) = 0.4307 and NPV = 12.1783.
criteria: V^U_0 = 86.9938, TS_1 = 0.2885 and TS_2 = 0.1868, based on D_0 and D_1 from (d).
Discounts the tax shields at r_U: PV(TS) = 0.4283. At r_D it would be 0.4441. Bonus, not required: saying why (the debt is rebalanced to a constant D/V).
NPV = −74 + 86.9938 + 0.4283 = 13.4221, the same as in (c). The answer is an NPV, so FCF_0 is included. With the fallback cash flows: PV(TS) = 0.4307, NPV = 12.1783.

parts.label: f
parts.body: A colleague subtracts the after-tax interest on the project's debt from each FCF and discounts at the WACC from (a). Is this right? Is the colleague's NPV too high or too low? Explain briefly.
parts.solution:
It is not right. The NPV is too low. The WACC method discounts unlevered free cash flows. The cost of debt, after tax, is already inside rwacc through the term (D/V)rD(1 − τ). Subtracting the interest from the cash flows as well counts the cost of debt twice, so every cash flow is too small and the NPV is understated.

For illustration (not required): with the debt from (d) the after-tax interest is 1.0228 in Year 1 and 0.6621 in Year 2, so the colleague's NPV is lower by 1.0228/1.0747 + 0.6621/1.07472 = 0.9517 + 0.5733 = 1.5250.

Cash flows after interest belong to the flow-to-equity method, which also adds net borrowing and discounts at rE to value the equity. The lecturer called subtracting interest from EBIT a big mistake people make in the exam (lecture 18).
criteria: Not right: the WACC method uses unlevered free cash flows, with no interest subtracted.
The after-tax cost of debt is already in r_wacc through (D/V)r_D(1 − τ), so subtracting interest counts it twice.
The colleague's NPV is too low.
Bonus, not required: flows after interest belong to the flow-to-equity method (plus net borrowing, discounted at r_E).

mk-ipo-1.title: Security issues
mk-ipo-1.merke: Samme form som IPO-eksemplet i forelesning 07
mk-ipo-1.body: Over the next year 100 small European tech firms will go public, one IPO at a time. The firms are independent and look identical to you. A firm's shares are worth either €55 (a good firm) or €34 (a bad firm) at the end of the first trading day, with equal probability. You are an uninformed investor and order 200 shares in every IPO. Some investors know each firm's type and order shares only in good IPOs: good IPOs are 8 times oversubscribed and bad IPOs 2.5 times. Oversubscribed IPOs are allocated pro rata. Everyone is risk neutral; ignore discounting within the day. Use 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.body: How many shares do you receive in a good and in a bad IPO? What is the expected value of a share?
parts.solution:
Good IPO: 200/8 = 25 shares. Bad IPO: 200/2.5 = 80 shares.

Expected value: 0.5 × 55 + 0.5 × 34 = €44.5. Without informed investors this would be the fair price and every IPO would give you an expected first-day return of 0%.
criteria: Allocations 200/8 = 25 and 200/2.5 = 80 shares.

parts.label: b
parts.body: Each IPO is priced at the expected value of a share. What is your average return (in %) on the shares you receive? (If you could not solve (a), use 30 shares in good IPOs, 70 in bad IPOs and a price of €45.)
parts.solution:
Over all 100 IPOs you expect 50 good and 50 bad ones, so you receive 50 × 25 = 1,250 good shares and 50 × 80 = 4,000 bad shares.

Profit = 1,250 × (55 − 44.5) + 4,000 × (34 − 44.5) = 13,125 − 42,000 = −28,875
Invested = 5,250 × 44.5 = 233,625

Return = −28,875/233,625 = −12.3596%

Even though half the IPOs are good, most of your shares are in bad ones. At this price you lose money and would stay away.

With the fallback numbers (30, 70 and €45): −10.4444%.
criteria: Weights the returns by the shares actually received: (1,250 × 10.5 − 4,000 × 10.5)/233,625 = −12.3596%.
Using the order of 200 shares in both types gives 0% and misses the point of the exercise.
Full marks with the fallback numbers: −10.4444%.
Show the calculation.

parts.label: c
parts.body: The allocations stay as in (a). At what issue price do you just break even, so that you are still willing to take part in every IPO? (If you could not solve (a), use 30 shares in good IPOs and 70 in bad.)
parts.solution:
Call the price X. Your expected profit over all IPOs must be zero:

1,250 × (55 − X) + 4,000 × (34 − X) = 0
68,750 + 136,000 = 5,250X
X = 204,750/5,250 = €39

The break-even price is the average value weighted by your allocations: (25 × 55 + 80 × 34)/(25 + 80) = 39, below the expected value of 44.5.

With the fallback allocations (30 and 70): X = (30 × 55 + 70 × 34)/100 = 40.3.
criteria: Sets up the break-even condition with the shares actually received, as the lecturer wrote it on the board.
X = 204,750/5,250 = €39. Using equal weights brings back the expected value of €44.5.
Full marks with the fallback allocations: X = €40.3.
Show the calculation.

parts.label: d
parts.body: Suppose every IPO is priced as in (c). What is the average first-day return across all IPOs? What return do the informed investors earn? What do you earn? (If you could not solve (c), use €41.)
parts.solution:
A good IPO rises from 39 to 55: 41.0256%. A bad IPO falls to 34: −12.8205%.

Average first-day return = 0.5 × 41.0256% + 0.5 × (−12.8205%) = 14.1026% (the same as 44.5/39 − 1).

The informed investors buy only good IPOs: 41.0256%. You break even: 0%, because the price was set to make you indifferent.

With the fallback €41: average 8.5366% and informed 34.1463%. You earn −4.8780% with the allocations from (a).
criteria: Average first-day return 14.1026%, the equal-weighted average of 41.0256% and −12.8205%.
Informed investors earn 41.0256% because they buy only good IPOs.
You earn 0%: the price is your break-even price.
Full marks with the fallback €41: 8.5366%, 34.1463% and −4.8780%.

parts.label: e
parts.body: A journalist writes: «IPOs rise sharply on the first day on average, so ordinary investors should buy every IPO. The underpricing shows that banks favour their hedge-fund clients.» Comment briefly on both claims.
parts.solution:
First claim: wrong. The average first-day return is earned by an investor who holds the same number of shares in every IPO. An uninformed investor cannot do that: in good IPOs the informed investors crowd in and you are rationed, while in bad IPOs nobody else bids and you get a large allocation. Your shares are tilted towards the bad IPOs, so you earn only 0%, not 14.1026%. This is the winner's curse.

Second claim: not needed. The underpricing follows from asymmetric information alone. Issuers need the uninformed investors, so they set the price where these just break even, below the expected value. The informed investors earn the gain, but the bank does not have to favour anyone. A conflict of interest at the bank is a possible extra explanation, but the lecturer's answer was that it is not the main one.
criteria: 2 points: the uninformed are rationed in good IPOs and get much more in bad ones, so they cannot earn the average first-day return; they earn 0% at this price.
2 points: underpricing arises even with an honest bank, because the price must let the uninformed break even (asymmetric information, the winner's curse).
Bonus, not required: mentioning the bank-conflict or insurance explanations as possible extra causes.
2 to 4 sentences are enough.

mk-ipo-2.title: Security issues
mk-ipo-2.merke: Samme form som IPO-eksemplet i forelesning 07, med etterspørselen oppgitt i aksjer
mk-ipo-2.body: A Norwegian bank arranges a series of IPOs of small firms. Each IPO sells 2 million new shares. A firm is good or bad with equal probability. Its shares are worth NOK 124 (good) or NOK 72 (bad) at the end of the first trading day. Informed investors know each firm's type: together they order 1.5 million shares in every good IPO and none in bad ones. Uninformed investors cannot tell the types apart and together order 2.5 million shares in every IPO, but they take part only if they expect at least to break even. All IPOs have the same price and oversubscribed IPOs are allocated pro rata. Everyone is risk neutral. Use 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.body: How many times is a good and a bad IPO oversubscribed? What fraction of an uninformed order is filled in each?
parts.solution:
Good IPO. Demand = 2.5 + 1.5 = 4 million against 2 million shares: 2 times oversubscribed, so each order is filled 2/4 = 50%.

Bad IPO. Only the uninformed bid: 2.5/2 = 1.25 times oversubscribed, filled 2/2.5 = 80%.
criteria: Good IPOs: demand 4 million, 2 times oversubscribed, fill rate 50%.
Bad IPOs: demand 2.5 million (the informed stay away), 1.25 times oversubscribed, fill rate 80%.
Leaving the informed demand out of the good IPOs gives the same fill rate in both and loses the points.

parts.label: b
parts.body: Every IPO is priced at the expected value of a share. What is the uninformed investors' average return on the shares they receive? (If you could not solve (a), use fill rates of 40% in good IPOs and 75% in bad IPOs.)
parts.solution:
Expected value: 0.5 × 124 + 0.5 × 72 = NOK 98.

Per pair of one good and one bad IPO the uninformed receive 0.5 × 2.5 = 1.25 million good shares and 0.8 × 2.5 = 2 million bad shares.

Profit = 1.25 × (124 − 98) + 2 × (72 − 98) = 32.5 − 52 = −19.5 (NOK million)
Invested = 3.25 × 98 = 318.5

Return = −19.5/318.5 = −6.1224%

With the fallback fill rates (40% and 75%): −8.0745%.
criteria: Price = expected value NOK 98.
Weights by the shares actually received (1.25 and 2 million per pair): return −6.1224%.
Full marks with the fallback fill rates: −8.0745%.
Show the calculation.

parts.label: c
parts.body: The bank wants every IPO to be fully subscribed. What is the highest price at which this happens?
parts.solution:
The informed investors order only 1.5 million shares and only in good IPOs, so every IPO needs the uninformed. They take part only if they at least break even, which pins down the price P:

1.25 × (124 − P) + 2 × (72 − P) = 0
155 + 144 = 3.25P
P = 299/3.25 = NOK 92

At any higher price the uninformed stay away: bad IPOs get no orders and good IPOs only 1.5 of the 2 million shares.

With the fallback fill rates: P = (1 × 124 + 1.875 × 72)/2.875 = 90.0870.
criteria: Sees that full subscription needs the uninformed, because informed demand is too small and absent from bad IPOs.
Sets the uninformed break-even condition with their allocations: P = 299/3.25 = NOK 92.
Full marks with the fallback fill rates: NOK 90.0870.
Swapping the fill rates gives NOK 104, above the expected value: a sign that something is wrong.

parts.label: d
parts.body: Suppose every IPO is priced as in (c). How much do the original owners leave on the table in a good and in a bad IPO (the first-day value of the shares sold minus the proceeds, which can be negative)? What is the average per IPO? What is the average first-day return? (If you could not solve (c), use NOK 90.)
parts.solution:
Good IPO: 2 × (124 − 92) = NOK 64 million. The buyers gain what the owners give up.

Bad IPO: 2 × (72 − 92) = −40: the owners of a bad firm receive NOK 40 million more than their shares are worth.

Average per IPO: 0.5 × 64 + 0.5 × (−40) = NOK 12 million (also 2 × (98 − 92) = 12).

Average first-day return = 98/92 − 1 = 6.5217%.

With the fallback NOK 90: 68, −36, average 16 and 8.8889%.
criteria: Good IPO: 2 × (124 − 92) = 64, so NOK 64 million is left on the table.
Bad IPO: 2 × (72 − 92) = −40: the owners receive NOK 40 million more than the shares are worth.
Average NOK 12 million per IPO = 2 × (98 − 92); average first-day return 6.5217%.
Full marks with the fallback NOK 90: 68, −36, 16 and 8.8889%.

parts.label: e
parts.body: Why can the bank not price every IPO at the expected value and sell only to the informed investors? Who bears the cost of the underpricing? Who gains? Explain briefly.
parts.solution:
The informed investors want only 1.5 million shares and only in good IPOs. The bank cannot tell the firms apart, so it needs the uninformed to fill every issue. The uninformed know they will be rationed in the good IPOs and filled in the bad ones, so they take part only at a price below the expected value, where they just break even.

The cost falls on the issuing firms' original owners, who sell for NOK 12 million less than the shares are worth on average. The informed investors gain: they buy good IPOs at 92 and own shares worth 124. The uninformed only break even.
criteria: 2 points: informed demand is too small and absent from bad IPOs, so the uninformed are needed. They take part only at their break-even price below the expected value (the winner's curse).
1 point: the cost falls on the original owners (money left on the table).
1 point: the informed investors gain.
Bonus, not required: the uninformed only break even.
2 to 4 sentences are enough.

mk-ipo-3.title: Security issues
mk-ipo-3.merke: Samme form som IPO-eksemplet i forelesning 07, med sannsynligheter som ikke er 50/50
mk-ipo-3.body: You plan to take part in the IPOs of 100 US biotech firms next year and order 100 shares in each. Each firm is good with probability 75% and bad with probability 25%, independently of the others. A good firm's shares are worth $30 at the end of the first trading day, a bad firm's $18. Informed investors bid only in good IPOs, so you receive 10% of the shares you order in a good IPO and 60% in a bad one. All IPOs have the same price. Everyone is risk neutral. Use 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.body: How many shares do you expect to receive in total in good IPOs and in bad IPOs?
parts.solution:
Good IPOs: 0.75 × 100 = 75 IPOs × 10 shares = 750 shares.
Bad IPOs: 0.25 × 100 = 25 IPOs × 60 shares = 1,500 shares.
criteria: 75 good IPOs × 10 shares = 750; 25 bad IPOs × 60 shares = 1,500.
Using 50 IPOs of each kind ignores the probabilities and loses the points.

parts.label: b
parts.body: What fraction of the shares you receive is in bad IPOs? Compare it with the fraction of IPOs that are bad and explain the difference in one sentence. (If you could not solve (a), use 800 shares in good IPOs and 1,200 in bad IPOs here and below.)
parts.solution:
Fraction in bad IPOs = 1,500/(750 + 1,500) = 1,500/2,250 = 66.6667%, against only 25% of the IPOs.

You are rationed hard in good IPOs, where the informed investors crowd in. In bad IPOs you bid almost alone and are largely filled. Getting a large allocation is itself bad news.

With the fallback numbers: 1,200/2,000 = 60.00%.
criteria: Fraction 1,500/2,250 = 66.6667% of your shares are in bad IPOs, against 25% of the IPOs.
One sentence on why: rationing in good IPOs (informed demand) and a much larger allocation in bad ones.
Full marks with the fallback numbers: 60.00%.

parts.label: c
parts.body: Every IPO is priced at the expected value of a share. What is your total expected profit? What is your return on the money you invest?
criteria: Price = expected value 0.75 × 30 + 0.25 × 18 = $27, not the 50/50 average of $24.
Full marks with the fallback numbers: −$8,400 and −15.5556%.

parts.label: d
parts.body: At what price do you just break even? At that price, what is the average first-day return across IPOs? What return do the informed investors earn?
parts.solution:
Step 1. Break-even. 750 × (30 − P) + 1,500 × (18 − P) = 0, so
P = (22,500 + 27,000)/2,250 = $22

Equivalently, P is the value weighted by your shares: 33.3333% × 30 + 66.6667% × 18 = 22.

Step 2. Returns. Average first-day return = 0.75 × (30/22 − 1) + 0.25 × (18/22 − 1) = 27/22 − 1 = 22.7273%. Informed investors: 30/22 − 1 = 36.3636%.

With the fallback numbers: P = (800 × 30 + 1,200 × 18)/2,000 = 22.8, average 18.4211% and informed 31.5789%.
criteria: Break-even price $22, from the shares actually received. Ignoring the probabilities gives $19.7143.
Average first-day return with the true probabilities 0.75 and 0.25: 22.7273%. Using 50/50 gives 9.0909%.
Informed investors 36.3636%.
Full marks with the fallback numbers: $22.8, 18.4211% and 31.5789%.
Show the calculation.

parts.label: e
parts.body: More investors become informed. You now receive only 5% of your order in good IPOs (still 60% in bad ones). Does your break-even price rise or fall? Who loses from the change and who gains? Explain briefly, without new calculations.
parts.solution:
It falls. With fewer good shares and as many bad ones, an even larger part of your shares is in bad IPOs, so you need a bigger discount to break even.

The issuing firms' original owners lose: to keep the uninformed in the market they must sell at a lower price and leave more money on the table. The informed investors gain, because they buy good IPOs at the lower price. You still break even.

For illustration (not required): 375 good and 1,500 bad shares give P = 20.4.
criteria: 2 points: the price falls, because the winner's curse gets worse (more of your shares in bad IPOs).
1 point: the original owners lose (more underpricing, more money left on the table).
1 point: the informed investors gain (as a group, or the newly informed).
Bonus, not required: the uninformed still only break even.
No calculation is needed.

mk-avvikle-1.title: Real options
mk-avvikle-1.merke: Samme form som butikkeksemplet med exit-klausul i forelesning 14
mk-avvikle-1.body: You can open a franchised salad bar in an office district in Lyon. The fit-out costs €250,000, paid today. Rent, staff and food cost €18,000 a month. Revenue will be either €21,500 a month forever (good demand) or €13,500 a month forever (bad demand), with equal probability. You learn which right after opening. All cash flows come at the end of each month, the first one month from today. Demand for salads is unrelated to the stock market, so discount at the risk-free rate of 5% per year. Use 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.body: What is the monthly discount rate?
parts.solution: rm = 1.051/12 − 1 = 0.004074 (0.4074%) per month. Dividing 5% by 12 ignores the compounding within the year.
criteria: 5%/12 = 0.4167% ignores the compounding within the year and loses the point.

parts.label: b
parts.body: What is the NPV of opening if you must run the bar forever? Do you open it? (If you could not solve (a), use 0.4% per month here and below.)
criteria: Expected net cash flow −500 a month, valued as a perpetuity at the monthly rate: NPV = −€372,725.78.
Decision: do not open.
Full marks with the fallback 0.4%: −€375,000.00.

parts.label: c
parts.body: The franchise contract lets you close the bar at no cost at the end of month 30, after that month's cash flow. After that you pay and receive nothing. What is the NPV of opening in the good and in the bad state?
parts.solution:
Good demand. You earn 3,500 a month and never close: NPV = −250,000 + 3,500/0.004074 = €609,080.43.

Bad demand. At month 30 you compare staying, which loses 4,500 a month forever, with closing, which gives 0. You close, so you lose money for 30 months only:

NPV = −250,000 − 4,500 × (1 − 1.004074−30)/0.004074 = −250,000 − 4,500 × 28.185169 = −€376,833.26

With the fallback 0.4%: 625,000.00 and −376,975.65.
criteria: Good state: a perpetuity of 3,500 a month, NPV = €609,080.43.
Bad state: compares staying with 0 and closes; an annuity of −4,500 for 30 months, NPV = −€376,833.26.
Keeping the bad state's loss as a perpetuity (−1,354,531.98) ignores the clause and loses the points.
Full marks with the fallback 0.4%: 625,000.00 and −376,975.65.

parts.label: d
parts.body: What is the NPV of opening with the clause? Do you open? What is the clause worth to you? (If you could not solve (c), use NPVs of €600,000 in the good state and −€380,000 in the bad state.)
parts.solution:
NPV = 0.5 × 609,080.43 + 0.5 × (−376,833.26) = €116,123.58. Positive: with the clause you open.

Without the clause your best choice is not to open, which is worth 0, not the negative NPV from (b). The clause is therefore worth €116,123.58: it turns a project you would reject into one worth that much.

With the fallback NPVs: 110,000 for both. With the fallback rate: 124,012.18.
criteria: NPV with the clause = €116,123.58; open.
Value of the clause = NPV with the clause − max(0, NPV without) = €116,123.58.
Subtracting the negative NPV from (b) (giving 488,849.36) treats a project you would never take as your alternative.
Full marks with the fallbacks: €110,000.00 or €124,012.18.

parts.label: e
parts.body: Without new calculations: how would the value of the clause change if you could close already after 12 months? What would the clause be worth if bad-demand revenue were €19,000 a month instead? Explain briefly.
parts.solution:
Exit after 12 months: worth more. The clause cuts off the losses of the bad state. With a shorter lock-in you suffer the €4,500 loss for 12 months instead of 30, so the bad-state NPV is less negative and the clause adds more value.

Bad-demand revenue of €19,000: worthless. Revenue would then exceed the running costs, so the bar earns money in both states and you would never use the right to close. An option you never exercise is worth nothing; its value comes only from avoiding losses.
criteria: 2 points: a shorter lock-in raises the value, because the losses in the bad state are cut off earlier.
2 points: with €19,000 the bad state earns money, you never close, so the clause is worth 0.
Bonus, not required: the general point that an exit option is valuable only where the continuation value is below 0.

mk-avvikle-2.title: Real options
mk-avvikle-2.merke: Samme form som H2025 E5 (d) og (e)
mk-avvikle-2.body: You can open an escape-room venue in Stavanger. Fitting out the rooms costs NOK 900,000, paid today. With good demand the venue earns NOK 150,000 a year forever; with bad demand it loses NOK 70,000 a year forever. Both are equally likely. You learn which right after opening. Cash flows come at the end of each year, the first one year from today. The risk is unrelated to the market, so discount at the risk-free rate of 6% a year.

parts.label: a
parts.body: What is the NPV of opening if you must run the venue forever? Do you open?

parts.label: b
parts.body: The landlord lets you close the venue at no cost at the end of Year 2, after that year's cash flow. After that you pay and receive nothing. What is the NPV of opening now? Do you open?
parts.solution:
Good demand: you never close. NPV = −900,000 + 150,000/0.06 = 1,600,000.00.

Bad demand: at the end of Year 2 the venue's remaining value is −70,000/0.06, below the 0 you get by closing, so you close. You lose 70,000 in Years 1 and 2 only:

NPV = −900,000 − 70,000/1.06 − 70,000/1.062 = −900,000.00 − 66,037.74 − 62,299.75 = −1,028,337.49

NPV of opening = 0.5 × 1,600,000.00 + 0.5 × (−1,028,337.49) = 800,000.00 − 514,168.74 = NOK 285,831.26. Positive, so you open.
criteria: Bad state: compares the continuation value with 0 and closes after Year 2: −1,028,337.49.
Using −70,000 forever in the bad state, or comparing with the negative value instead of 0, is the mistake the lecturer warned about.

parts.label: c
parts.body: What is the right to close worth to you? (If you could not solve (b), use an NPV of NOK 300,000.)
parts.solution:
Without the right your best choice is not to open (0). With it the project is worth 285,831.26. The right is worth NOK 285,831.26.

Subtracting the negative NPV from (a) instead gives 519,164.59, which values the right against a project you would never take. With the fallback: NOK 300,000.
criteria: Value = NPV with the right − max(0, NPV without) = 285,831.26.
Using the negative NPV from (a) as the alternative (519,164.59) loses the point.
Full marks with the fallback: 300,000.

parts.label: d
parts.body: Keep the right to close at the end of Year 2. Suppose the yearly cash flow is 40,000 + X with good demand and 40,000 − X with bad demand. For which X are you indifferent about opening?
criteria: Sets up the indifference condition with the exit after Year 2 in the bad state.
Treating the bad state as a perpetuity (no exit) gives no solution with a positive NPV and loses the points.
Show the calculation.

parts.label: e
parts.body: In (d) a larger X leaves the expected yearly cash flow unchanged. Why does it still make opening more attractive? Explain briefly.
parts.solution: Because of the right to close, the two states are treated differently. A larger X raises the good state's cash flow forever but lowers the bad state's only for two years, since you then close. The upside grows while the downside is capped, so more spread means more value. The right to close is an option; options are worth more when uncertainty is larger.
criteria: 2 points: the upside is kept forever while the downside is cut off after two years.
1 point: the right to close is an option; options gain value with more uncertainty (spread).
2 to 3 sentences are enough.

mk-avvikle-3.title: Real options
mk-avvikle-3.merke: Samme form som exit-eksemplet i forelesning 14 og 18, med kvartalsvise kontantstrømmer
mk-avvikle-3.body: A US mattress brand can open a showroom in a Denver mall. The fit-out costs $600,000, paid today. Rent, staff and other costs are $90,000 a quarter. Revenue will be $130,000 a quarter forever with probability 45% (good demand) or $60,000 a quarter forever with probability 55% (bad demand). The brand learns which right after opening. Cash flows come at the end of each quarter, the first one quarter from today. Demand is unrelated to the market, so discount at the risk-free rate of 8% a year. Use 4 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.body: What is the quarterly discount rate?
criteria: 8%/4 = 2% ignores the compounding within the year and loses the point.

parts.label: b
parts.body: What is the NPV of opening if the brand must keep the showroom forever? Does it open? (If you could not solve (a), use 2% per quarter here and below.)
criteria: Expected net cash flow +1,500 a quarter; NPV = −522,786.07; do not open.
Using 50/50 instead of 45/55 is an error.
Full marks with the fallback 2%: −525,000.00.

parts.label: c
parts.body: The mall offers a lease that lets the brand leave at the end of quarter 6, after that quarter's cash flow, if it pays an exit fee of $50,000 then. After that it pays and receives nothing. Does the brand leave with bad demand? What is the NPV of opening in each state and in total? Does it open?
criteria: Exit decision: compares staying (a perpetuity of −30,000) with paying the fee, not with 0; leaves.
Good state 1,459,038.09; bad state −812,917.25, with the fee discounted from quarter 6.
Total NPV 209,462.65; open.
Forgetting the fee gives −768,368.62 in the bad state.

parts.label: d
parts.body: What is the largest exit fee at which the brand would still leave with bad demand at the end of quarter 6? Explain what you compare.
parts.solution:
At the end of quarter 6 the brand compares the value of staying with the cost of leaving. Staying is worth −30,000/0.019427 = −1,544,278.57. It leaves as long as the fee is smaller than that loss: the largest fee is $1,544,278.57.

The fit-out cost and the losses of the first six quarters play no role: they are already spent. Only the cash flows from quarter 7 on are compared.

With the fallback 2%: 1,500,000.00.
criteria: Largest fee = present value at quarter 6 of the future losses = 30,000/0.019427 = 1,544,278.57.
Says what is compared: staying (the perpetuity of losses) against paying the fee and leaving.
Full marks with the fallback 2%: 1,500,000.00.

parts.label: e
parts.body: At the end of quarter 6, with bad demand, the brand's founder says: «We have spent $600,000 on this showroom. If we leave now, that money is lost, so we should stay until we earn it back.» Comment briefly.
parts.solution: The founder is wrong. The $600,000 is a sunk cost: it is gone whether the brand stays or leaves, so it must not affect the decision. Only the future matters: staying loses $30,000 a quarter forever (worth −1,544,279), leaving costs $50,000. With bad demand the showroom never earns the money back, so staying only adds to the losses. Treat the present as given and take the best decision from here.
criteria: 2 points: the fit-out cost is sunk and irrelevant for the decision at quarter 6.
2 points: compares only future cash flows (stay: losses forever; leave: the fee), so the brand should leave.
2 to 4 sentences are enough.

mk-ma-motiver-1.title: M&A
mk-ma-motiver-1.merke: Samme form som H2024 E1, med synergier utelukket som i forelesning 16 og 18
mk-ma-motiver-1.body: Give three reasons for an acquisition other than synergies (gains from running the two firms' operations together): (i) one where the acquirer creates value by changing how the target is run, (ii) one where the acquirer's shareholders gain at the expense of someone else and (iii) one that is not in the interest of the acquirer's shareholders. Explain the mechanism behind each reason in 1-2 sentences; naming a reason or writing «value creation» is not enough (3 points per reason). Finally, explain in one sentence why buying a firm to use its accumulated tax losses does not count as a reason (1 point).
mk-ma-motiver-1.solution:
(i) Replacing inefficient management (a disciplinary takeover). If the target is badly run, its price reflects that; the acquirer buys it, installs better managers and runs the same assets more efficiently, so the gain comes from better management, not from combining operations.

(ii) Market power. Buying a competitor reduces competition, so the merged firm can raise prices or pay suppliers less; the acquirer's shareholders gain, but the value comes from customers and suppliers rather than from new value created.

(iii) Managerial ambition (empire building). A CEO whose pay, power or prestige grows with the size of the firm may buy targets that do not pay off for the shareholders, often overpaying; the lecturer's example was the purchase of Twitter. This is an agency problem: the shareholders bear the cost.

Tax losses. Accumulated tax losses are erased when a firm changes owner, so the acquirer cannot use them (lecture 17).

Also accepted. (i) more efficient practices or better access to markets for the target; (ii) buying an undervalued target with better information, or buying a distressed target cheaply; (iii) hubris and the winner's curse, buying to meet a KPI or to inflate earnings per share, diversification that the shareholders could do themselves.
criteria: 3 points per reason: 1 for a reason in the right category, 2 for the mechanism in 1-2 sentences.
(i) must change how the target is run (new management, better practices). Economies of scale or cost savings from merging departments are synergies and score nothing here.
(ii) must say who loses (customers, suppliers or the target's sellers). Market power, an undervalued target or a distressed target are accepted.
(iii) must be against the acquirer's shareholders' interest and name the mechanism (agency problem, overconfidence, overpaying). «Value creation» or a reason without a mechanism scores nothing.
1 point: tax losses are erased on a change of owner, so they are not a motive.
Two answers that rest on the same mechanism count once.

mk-ma-motiver-2.title: M&A
mk-ma-motiver-2.merke: Samme form som teorispørsmålene i forelesning 16 om hvem som vinner
mk-ma-motiver-2.body:
Westerly Foods (A) is worth $800 million and Kellan Organics (T) $200 million on their own. A agrees to buy T for $290 million in cash and expects synergies of $100 million.

a) How are the expected gains split between A's and T's shareholders? Why does the target usually capture most of the synergies? (4 points; 2-3 sentences)

b) Suppose instead that T had been close to default: its owners' alternative to selling was bankruptcy and A could have bought it for $215 million (same stand-alone value and synergies). How would the gains have been split? Why? (3 points; 1-2 sentences)

c) When the deal is announced, A's share price falls. Give one reason why this can happen even though A's managers expect synergies of $100 million. (3 points; 1-2 sentences)
mk-ma-motiver-2.solution:
a) T's shareholders gain P − T = 290 − 200 = $90 million; A's gain S − (P − T) = 100 − 90 = $10 million. The two add up to the synergies. The target captures most because it can say no: its owners keep a firm worth $200 million unless they are paid more. With competing bidders the price is pushed towards T + S. The bid also tells the market that T is worth more than it thought, so T's price jumps.

b) T would gain only 215 − 200 = $15 million and A $85 million. A distressed target has lost its bargaining power: refusing means bankruptcy, so the acquirer can keep most of the synergies.

c) The market may not believe the synergies: if investors expect less than the $90 million premium, A overpays and its value falls. Also accepted: the market reads the deal as empire building or hubris, or fears problems integrating the firms (for example the corporate culture).
criteria: a) 2 points for the split: T + 90, A + 10, summing to S = 100.
a) 2 points for why: the target can refuse (bargaining power), competition among bidders, the bid signals the target is worth more.
b) 1 point for the split (T + 15, A + 85), 2 points for why: the target in distress has no bargaining power, so the acquirer captures most of the synergies.

c) 3 points for one reason with its mechanism: the market expects synergies below the premium (overpayment), empire building or hubris, integration costs. «The market is negative» without a reason scores nothing.

mk-ma-motiver-3.title: M&A
mk-ma-motiver-3.merke: Samme form som kontanter mot aksjer i forelesning 16
mk-ma-motiver-3.body:
Oakridge Software (A) is worth €700 million and will buy Pellow Analytics (T), worth €200 million on its own. The expected synergies are €100 million. A can pay €250 million in cash or give T's shareholders new A shares that make up 25% of the combined firm.

a) How are the expected gains split between A's and T's shareholders under each offer? (2 points)

b) After the deal the synergies turn out to be only €40 million. What is the gain or loss for A's and T's shareholders under each offer? Who bears the synergy risk? (4 points; 1-2 sentences for the explanation)

c) Give one reason why A's managers might prefer to pay in shares that the market would dislike. Give one reason why T's owners might insist on cash. (4 points; 1-2 sentences each)
mk-ma-motiver-3.solution:
a) Cash: T gains 250 − 200 = 50 and A gains 1,000 − 250 − 700 = 50. Shares: T owns 0.25 × 1,000 = 250 and gains 50; A keeps 0.75 × 1,000 = 750 and gains 50. At the expected synergies the split is the same, €50 million each.

b) The combined firm is worth 940. Cash: T still gains 50, A gains 940 − 250 − 700 = −10. Shares: T gains 0.25 × 940 − 200 = 35 and A 0.75 × 940 − 700 = 5. With cash the target's payment is fixed, so A's shareholders bear all of the synergy risk; with shares the shortfall is shared in proportion to ownership (25% for T, 75% for A).

c) A's managers may pay in shares because they think A's shares are overvalued: paying with expensive paper is cheap for A, but the market knows this and reads a share offer as a sign of overvaluation, so A's price falls. T's owners may insist on cash because they want to leave and spend the money, or because they doubt the value of A's shares and do not want to carry the risk of A and of the synergies. Also accepted: A has cash it does not need (A prefers cash); the target's founders want to stay on and share in the firm (they prefer shares, the opposite case).
criteria: a) 2 points: both offers give T + 50 and A + 50 at the expected synergies.
b) 2 points for the numbers: cash T + 50, A −10; shares T + 35, A + 5.
b) 2 points: with cash the acquirer bears all the synergy risk; with shares it is shared in proportion to ownership.
c) 2 points for A: overvalued shares (paying with expensive paper), with the market reading it as a negative signal.
c) 2 points for T: wants liquidity or to exit, or doubts the value of A's shares and the synergies. A reason without a mechanism scores 1 point.
